label: Geodesics; Convex Neighborhoods
notes: This chapter spans printed pages sixty through eighty-seven and turns the Riemannian connection into a theory of preferred curves. We define geodesics as curves of zero acceleration, then build the exponential map and prove that short geodesics are the shortest paths inside convex neighborhoods of the manifold.

label: The Geodesic Equation
notes: A geodesic is a curve whose velocity is parallel along itself, so its covariant acceleration vanishes identically. In a coordinate chart this becomes a second order system coupling the coordinates through the Christoffel symbols, and existence theory for ODEs gives a unique geodesic from each prescribed initial position and velocity.

label: The Geodesic Flow
notes: Lifting the second order geodesic equation to the tangent bundle produces a first order vector field whose integral curves are exactly the geodesics. This geodesic field generates a flow on the tangent bundle, and smooth dependence on initial data ensures geodesics vary smoothly with both their starting point and their starting velocity.

label: Homogeneity of Geodesics
notes: Rescaling the initial velocity rescales the geodesic in time by the same factor, so a geodesic traversed twice as fast covers the same image curve in half the time. This homogeneity property lets us shrink any tangent vector until the corresponding geodesic is defined on the full unit interval.

label: The Exponential Map
notes: The exponential map sends a tangent vector to the point reached at time one along the geodesic leaving the base point in that direction. It is defined on an open neighborhood of the origin of the tangent space, depends smoothly on its argument, and packages the entire geodesic spray into a single map.

label: Local Diffeomorphism
notes: The derivative of the exponential map at the origin is the identity, so by the inverse function theorem it restricts to a diffeomorphism from a small ball in the tangent space onto a normal neighborhood of the base point. This is the precise sense in which geodesics deliver honest local coordinates.

label: Normal Coordinates
notes: Pulling coordinates back through the inverse exponential map gives normal coordinates centered at the point. In these coordinates the metric agrees with the identity at the center, all Christoffel symbols vanish there, and radial straight lines through the origin become the geodesics emanating from that point, which simplifies many local computations.

label: The Gauss Lemma
notes: The Gauss lemma states that the image of a sphere in the tangent space meets the radial geodesics orthogonally. Equivalently, geodesics leaving a point stay perpendicular to the geodesic spheres surrounding it, which is the geometric key that lets us discard angular motion in the minimizing argument coming next.

label: Geodesics Minimize Locally
notes: Inside a normal ball the radial geodesic from the center to a point is strictly shorter than every other piecewise smooth curve joining them. The proof splits a competing curve into radial and angular components and uses the Gauss lemma to discard the angular contribution as length wasted off the direct path.

label: The Minimizing Estimate
notes: Writing a competing curve in polar geodesic coordinates, its length integral dominates the integral of the radial speed, which already equals the geodesic distance between the endpoints. Equality forces the angular part to vanish and the radius to increase monotonically, so only the radial geodesic actually achieves the shortest possible length.

label: Totally Normal Neighborhoods
notes: A totally normal neighborhood is one contained in a normal ball of each of its own points, so any two points inside it are joined by a unique minimizing geodesic that stays within. Such neighborhoods exist around every point of the manifold, established by a uniform continuity argument applied to the exponential map.

label: Convex Neighborhoods
notes: A neighborhood is convex when the connecting geodesic between any two of its points lies entirely within it. Bounding the second derivative of squared distance along geodesics shows that sufficiently small geodesic balls are strictly convex, which completes the local picture of geodesics as uniquely determined, well behaved shortest paths.
